title: Calculating acute:chronic workload ratios using exponentially weighted moving averages provides a more sensitive indicator of injury likelihood than rolling averages
authors: Murray NB, Gabbett TJ, Townshend AD, Blanch P
population: 59 elite Australian football players from one club over 2 years (GPS external load, non-contact time-loss injuries)
findings: ACWR values differed significantly between rolling-average and EWMA models in the moderate (1.0-1.49, p=0.021), high (1.50-1.99, p=0.012) and very high (>2.0, p=0.001) ranges.

Both models showed significant associations between a very high ACWR (>2.0) and injury risk for total distance (RR 6.52-21.28) and high-speed distance (RR 5.87-13.43); the EWMA model was more sensitive.
The variance (R2) in injury explained was significantly greater with the EWMA model.
limitations: Team-sport athletes, one club, injury (not performance) outcome, associational. Contradicted for runners by nakaoka-2021-acwr-runners and criticised conceptually by impellizzeri-2020-acwr-pitfalls. The abstract states no EWMA decay constants.
implications: If an acute/chronic metric is computed, use EWMA weighting rather than uncoupled rolling windows, but present it only as descriptive context.
No specific EWMA decay constants can be justified from this abstract.

verification.notes: Crossref issued online 2016-12-21 (Europe PMC lists 2017 print); kept 2017. Numbers match Europe PMC abstract.
